Leipzig ist alt — schon im Jahre 1015 ist die Stadt dokumentiert. Es ist auch eine Stadt von großer historischer Bedeutung: Napoleon hat hier gekämpft°, J.S. Die Stadt hat ihre größte Entwicklung im 19. Jahrhundert erlebt°. Damals sind so viele Menschen in die Stadt gezogen, dass die Bevölkerung von 32.000 auf 450.000 gewachsen ist.

Drei Ereignisse im 20. Jahrhundert haben das Gesicht von Leipzig stark verändert:

Am 4. Dezember 1943 haben die Engländer die Stadt stark bombardiert und viel zerstört° — vor allem in der Innenstadt .

8.5

A. Subject-verb inversion


A.1

Whether you've noticed them or not, you’ve encountered literally hundreds of examples of a grammatical structure in German that differs markedly from English:

Manchmal essen wir bei McDonald’s.

Im 19. Jahrhundert ist Leipzig viel größer geworden.

Auf Instagram gibt es viele Storys.

Diese Filme nennt man »Heimatfilme«.

In der DDR waren die alten Autos teurer als neue Modelle.

Den ganzen Sommer müssen die Fans auf den ersten Spieltag warten.


What's the difference? Word order. Notice how the elements in the first German sentence are sequenced as compared with its English translation:

Manchmal essen wir bei McDonald’s.

Sometimes we eat at McDonald’s.

Both sentences begin with a time element: Manchmal ... / Sometimes ..., but whereas English continues with the usual subject/verb pattern ( ... we eat ...), German inverts that pattern and places the subject after the verb: ... essen wir ... .

Looking at the other examples, you can see that this holds true regardless of whether the initial element is a one-word element (Manchmal …), two words (Auf Instagram … / Diese Filme …), or even longer (Im 19. Jahrhundert … / In der DDR … / Den ganzen Sommer …). You’ll also notice that these elements have various functions — some are adverbial modifiers of time and place, and one of them is a direct object (Diese Filme).

The important difference here is that German allows only one such element to appear before the conjugated verb, in what is often called the “front field” of the sentence. And if that element is not the subject, then the subject must come after the verb. To put it another way: The conjugated verb must always be the second element.

This rule is easy enough to articulate — but it turns out to be relatively difficult to put into practice for learners whose native language doesn’t follow this pattern. English speakers are so used to stating the subject before the verb, no matter how much information precedes it, that they instinctively do so in German as well. (And even non-native speakers of English tend to stumble over this when they learn German.)

content:
A.2

Coordinating conjunctions


This rule about verb placement pertains to units of ideas known as independent clauses. So far, each of the examples and exercises in this section has made use of a single independent clause:

Manchmal essen wir bei McDonald’s.

Auf Instagram gibt es viele Storys.

In der DDR waren die alten Autos teurer als neue Modelle.


But independent clauses are routinely joined together by way of words such as und, aber, denn and oder, which are known as coordinating conjunctions. These conjunctions do not affect the word order within the clauses they connect; they simply tie them together. In other words, an independent clause following und, aber, denn and oder begins with its own first element, not the conjugated verb:

Manchmal essen wir bei McDonald’s, und dann bestelle ich mir einen Big Mac mit Pommes.

Auf Instagram gibt es viele Storys, aber natürlich sind nicht alle ganz echt.

In der DDR waren die alten Autos teurer als neue Modelle, denn man musste so lang auf die neuen Modelle warten.

content:
B. Review

Beginning with this section, the Strukturen in Chapter 8 provide focused grammar reviews of the concepts you’ve learned so far. By definition, a “focused” review can’t include everything. And because the reviews reach across chapter boundaries to bring together various aspects of these grammar points, certain vocabulary items — prepositions and modal verbs, for example — will appear out of sequence compared with the comprehensive vocabulary reviews that appear in Thema 3 and Thema 4 of this chapter. Nonetheless, we think these reviews will be helpful, and we encourage you to work through them carefully.


B.1

Grammatical Case

You’ve been introduced to three of the four grammatical cases in German and the various functions they take on:

  1. Nominative

    • the default case for nouns (i.e., when they stand alone, with no grammatical context)

    • indicates the subject of a sentence

    • used with nouns referring to the sentence subject, following verbs such as these:

      sein to be
      werden to become
      bleiben to remain, stay
      gelten + als considered to be

  2. Accusative

    • indicates the direct object

    • used with accusative prepositions:

      durch / für / gegen / ohne / um

    • used with variable prepositions in contexts showing motion toward a destination:

      an / auf / unter / über / hinter / vor / neben / zwischen / in

    • used as the object of es gibt: There is … / There are …


  3. Dative

    • used with dative prepositions:

      ab / aus / außer / bei / gegenüber / mit / nach / seit / von / zu

    • used with variable prepositions in contexts showing location:

      an / auf / unter / über / hinter / vor / neben / zwischen / in

    • indicates the recipient (i.e., the indirect object) of something:

      (in conjunction with verbs such as geben / schicken / zeigen / erklären)

    • used with objects of dative verbs:

      antworten / glauben (people) / helfen / gefallen / gehören

B.2

der-words


The options in Übung 8.5 above should remind you of an important difference between der-words and ein-words:

das / ein Mitglied

der / ein Beruf

In the nominative case, der-words distinguish between masculine and neuter nouns, while ein-words do not. The discussion below reviews the ways that this works out in all three grammatical cases, and for all the words that follow the patterns of der-words and ein-words, respectively.

Der-words distinguish the three genders in the nominative case with endings that correspond to the definite articles:

der → -er die → -e das → -es

You’ve learned four der-words that use these endings:

dies- this (sing.) / these (pl.)

jed- every (sing. only)

welch- which

all- all (plural only)
